youtubeTitle: The Gospel and Soul Health Session 34 - Dr Bruce Wauchope
topic: Dropping defences: self-acceptance and the embodied soul
summary: Bruce continues the overview of soul healing. When people stop striving and walk with Jesus within, others in the religious system may accuse them of backsliding, which family-systems theory explains as the system reacting to one member's change. Against the Neoplatonic programme of escaping the body, Jesus is enfleshed: present in our bodies and in our darkness, even in our acting-out behaviours, which enables people to embrace a healthy embodied sexuality. As guilt, separation and striving drop, the wall between 'good' and 'bad' parts falls and self-acceptance emerges, illustrated by a woman with severe dissociation who discovered her split-off parts. Defences dropping means insecurity, abandonment, fear, shame and grief resurface, and this is a decision point: go back or continue. The Hebrew soul (nephesh) is the body, so emotions are processed bodily; healing involves facing body and emotions, often with community or counselling support.
keyPoints: The 'institution' that calls itself church often creates vertical power, the opposite of the gospel's serving; ekklesia means the called-out community of believers.
When someone stops performing religious activities and walks with Jesus inside, others may accuse them of backsliding, because their change threatens the system that justifies them.
Family-systems theory: when one member changes, the whole system goes up and down; this is a healthy discombobulation, like Christ disturbing us from within.
Neoplatonic spirituality says acknowledge, confess, repent, renounce, live holy and escape the body; but Jesus is enfleshed, in our human body and in our human darkness.

As a doctor counselling men caught in pornography, Bruce asks whether they can recognise Jesus present even in their sexual acting-out; knowing he is there makes it possible to embrace the body and sexuality in a healthy way.

Loss of guilt brings assurance, loss of separation brings union, loss of striving brings rest, and then the wall between our 'good' and 'bad' parts, a separation invented by the tree of death, begins to fall.
Jesus wants every crumb of us, as at the feeding of the five thousand: gather up the fragments so nothing is lost.

A woman found money withdrawn from her account by herself, on ATM footage, with no memory, and two wardrobes of clothes: severe childhood trauma had split her into dissociated parts; we all have the same splitting at a lower level.
We hide from parts of ourselves like children covering their eyes, thinking God can't see what we won't look at; yet Jesus has been holding those parts all along.
As defences drop, insecurity, abandonment, rejection, fear, guilt, shame and grief return; this is a decision tree where we can go back or continue.
In Hebrew thinking the soul (nephesh) is the body: 'my soul cries out' means my organs cry out; we process emotion in the whole body (somatic therapy; van der Kolk's The Body Keeps the Score).
Real inner work can happen through ordinary community or counselling; when well-meaning people accuse you, there is another junction: re-erect your conscience and defences, or continue the walk.

keyTerms.definition: The called-out community of believers, as opposed to an institution of vertical power.
The idea that when one member of a relational system changes, the whole system reacts.
Christ present both in our human body and in our human darkness (flesh).
Owning all of oneself as the false wall between good and bad parts drops.
Split-off aspects of the self formed in response to trauma, in extreme cases with memory gaps.
The Hebrew word for soul, meaning the whole embodied person, including organs.
The junction where resurfacing pain or accusation tempts us back to defences or invites us to keep walking.

quotes: Jesus is in me in the places I don't like.
Let no bit be lost; gather every little crumb of every single human.
In Hebrew, the soul is your body.
Is Jesus there the whole time? Yes, holding that part of you.

nodes.label: Guilt and striving drop

nodes.label: Good/bad wall falls
nodes.detail: The mythical split between acceptable and unacceptable parts dissolves.

nodes.label: Self-acceptance emerges
nodes.detail: We look at ourselves with open eyes, knowing Jesus held every part.

nodes.label: Buried pain resurfaces
nodes.detail: Fear, shame, abandonment and grief come back up.

nodes.label: Decision point
nodes.detail: Rebuild defences and conscience, or continue walking.

diagram.note: Bruce's overview of the middle stage of healing, with the key junction where we may slip back into defences.

caseStudy.title: Accused of backsliding
caseStudy.scenario: Tom stopped attending several church programmes after discovering a quieter walk with Jesus within. Some friends tell him he's drifting. At the same time, he's noticing feelings of abandonment from childhood he'd never let himself feel, and tension in his chest when they come up. He's tempted to go back to the busy routine that kept him from feeling.
caseStudy.analysis: Tom's change is unsettling his relational system, which reacts with accusation. Meanwhile his defences are dropping and buried pain is surfacing in his body, the Hebrew sense of the soul. He has reached Bruce's decision tree: rebuild his defences or keep walking.
pathway: Recognise friends' reactions as a system responding to change, and answer graciously without defending himself.
Remember Jesus has been holding the abandoned part all along.
Pay attention to where emotion sits in his body and breathe with it.
Find a safe group or counsellor (possibly somatic) to help him process.
When tempted to retreat into busyness, name the choice and ask the Spirit for courage to continue.

practices.name: Body check-in
practices.how: Three times a day pause, scan from head to belly, and notice where emotion is sitting. Name it and invite Jesus to be present there.

practices.name: Gather the crumbs
practices.how: Write down one part of yourself you prefer to hide. Pray: 'Jesus, you want every crumb of me; I let you hold this part.'

practices.name: Name the junction
practices.how: When pain or criticism makes you want to tighten up, say: 'This is a junction; I choose to keep walking with you.'

reflection: Which parts of yourself do you keep behind a wall marked 'bad'?
Where in your body do you tend to carry stress or grief?
How do people around you react when you change, and how might you respond with love?

quiz.q: What does the Hebrew word nephesh (soul) emphasise?
options: The whole embodied person, including organs
quiz.explain: In Hebrew thought the soul is the body.

quiz.q: Why might others accuse someone of backsliding when they stop striving?
options: Their change threatens the system others rely on
They really are drifting from God
quiz.explain: Family-systems theory: one member's change unsettles the whole system.

quiz.q: What happens as the wall between good and bad parts falls?
options: Buried pain such as fear, shame and grief resurfaces
quiz.explain: Defences dropping lets suppressed pain come back up for healing.
